summary: This draft-standard memo documents version 2 of OSPF, a link-state routing protocol run within a single autonomous system. Routers hold identical topology databases and compute shortest-path trees, recalculating quickly after changes. It was replaced by RFC 2328.

eli5.summary: Every router has the same map of the roads and finds the shortest way itself.

subtitle: A link-state routing protocol for TCP/IP internets using shortest path first calculations

tldr.problem: Routers in an Autonomous System need a dynamic routing protocol that quickly detects topology changes and minimizes routing traffic while maintaining consistent routing decisions across the network.
tldr.mechanism: OSPF makes every router maintain an identical link-state database describing the network topology, then each router independently runs the Shortest Path First algorithm to calculate optimal routes to all destinations.
tldr.outcome: OSPF provides fast convergence, efficient use of bandwidth, support for areas to hide topology complexity, and authentication of routing updates. It was replaced by RFC 2328.

today: RFC 2178 is a Standards Track specification from 1997 describing OSPF version 2. This RFC has been superseded by RFC 2328, which is the current standard for OSPF version 2 and includes additional clarifications, corrections, and refinements. While RFC 2178 and RFC 2328 differ only in clarifications and are backward-compatible, implementations should use RFC 2328.

sections.title: Overview: How OSPF Works
sections.content:
OSPF is an Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) designed to distribute routing information between routers within a single Autonomous System. It is fundamentally different from earlier distance-vector protocols like RIP: instead of telling neighbors a summary of distances, OSPF routers exchange complete information about the network topology and each router independently calculates the best routes using the Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm, also known as Dijkstra's algorithm. This means OSPF routers have an identical view of the network and make routing decisions based on the same data.

The OSPF protocol is classified as link-state technology because routers advertise the state of their connections (links) rather than distances to destinations. Each router builds a database of link-state advertisements from all other routers, giving it a complete directed graph of the network. From this graph, each router calculates a tree of shortest paths with itself at the root, yielding its routing table.
sections.eli5: Every router gets a complete map of the network topology, then calculates the shortest path to every place using the same algorithm. Since they all start with the same map, they all make the same routing choices.

sections.title: Key Concepts: Routers, Neighbors, and Adjacencies
sections.content:
In OSPF, neighboring routers are those connected to a common network. The Hello Protocol runs continuously on every interface to discover neighbors and maintain neighbor relationships. Two neighbors form an adjacency when they are selected to exchange detailed routing information; not all neighbors become adjacent. This reduction in adjacencies saves bandwidth and reduces the size of the link-state database.

Routers are assigned a 32-bit Router ID that uniquely identifies them within the AS. Networks are classified as point-to-point (connecting exactly two routers), broadcast (like Ethernet, supporting many routers with broadcast capability), or non-broadcast (like Frame Relay, supporting many routers without broadcast). OSPF handles each type differently: broadcast and non-broadcast networks elect a Designated Router to generate network advertisements and reduce the number of adjacencies.
sections.eli5: Routers say hello to their neighbors on all their connections. Some neighbors become friends (adjacencies) and share detailed map updates. On networks with many routers, one router is elected to represent the network to reduce chatter.

sections.title: The Link-State Database and Network Graph
sections.content:
The heart of OSPF is the link-state database, which every router in an area maintains identically. This database is built from link-state advertisements (LSAs) flooded throughout the area. Each router originates one router-LSA describing its interfaces and neighbors. On broadcast and non-broadcast networks, the Designated Router originates a network-LSA listing the routers attached to the network. Area border routers originate summary-LSAs to summarize routes between areas, and AS boundary routers originate AS-external-LSAs to advertise routes to other Autonomous Systems.

The database forms a directed graph where vertices are routers and networks, and edges represent connections with associated costs. Each router can examine this graph and build its own shortest-path tree, guaranteeing loop-free routing and identical routing decisions within an area.
sections.eli5: Every router has a database with the same list of all the roads and how much they cost to use. Each road is described by the router it belongs to or by the network it is on. This shared database lets every router calculate the same routes.

sections.title: Dividing Networks into Areas
sections.content:
OSPF allows splitting an Autonomous System into areas, groups of contiguous networks and hosts. Each area runs its own separate copy of the SPF algorithm, maintaining its own link-state database. The topology of an area is hidden from outside it, reducing routing traffic and protecting the area from bad routing data injected elsewhere.

The special OSPF area 0 (the backbone) connects all other areas and is responsible for distributing inter-area routing information. Area border routers connect to multiple areas, summarizing the topology of each attached area for distribution via the backbone. Routers within a single area need only know detailed topology within that area; inter-area routes are summarized by area border routers. Virtual links can be configured between area border routers to maintain backbone connectivity when physical connectivity is broken.
sections.eli5: A large network can be divided into sections so routers in one section do not need to know every detail about other sections. One special section (the backbone) connects all the others and passes summaries of routing information between them.

sections.title: Discovering and Maintaining Neighbors via Hello Protocol
sections.content:
The Hello Protocol is OSPF's mechanism for discovering neighbors and detecting dead routers. Routers send Hello packets at regular intervals to the multicast address AllSPFRouters on broadcast and point-to-point networks, or to configured neighbors on non-broadcast networks. Each Hello packet carries the sender's Router ID, a list of known neighbors, and optional parameters like the Hello interval and dead timer.

A router that receives Hello packets from a neighbor knows the neighbor is reachable. If a router stops receiving Hellos from a neighbor within the dead interval, that neighbor is considered unreachable and all adjacencies to it are torn down, triggering a recalculation of the routing table. On broadcast networks, the Hello Protocol also elects the Designated Router and Backup Designated Router based on router priority and Router ID.
sections.eli5: Routers keep saying hello to each other. If one router stops hearing hellos from another, it assumes that router has crashed and recalculates all routes without it.

sections.title: Link-State Advertisements and Their Types
sections.content:
Link-state advertisements come in five types. Router-LSAs are originated by every router and describe the state of the router's interfaces to an area, including costs to attached networks. Network-LSAs are originated by the Designated Router on broadcast and NBMA networks, listing the routers attached to the network. Summary-LSAs (types 3 and 4) originate from area border routers: type 3 describes routes to networks outside the area, and type 4 describes routes to AS boundary routers. AS-external-LSAs originate from AS boundary routers and describe routes to destinations outside the AS.

Each LSA carries a sequence number and age. When multiple copies of an LSA exist, the one with the higher sequence number is considered newer. The age field is incremented as the LSA is flooded, and when age reaches the maximum value the LSA is discarded from the database.
sections.eli5: Each router creates messages describing its connections. Big networks create messages listing which routers are attached. Boundary routers create summaries of distant places. These messages travel from router to router like a game of telephone, but the newest version always wins.

sections.title: Flooding and Database Synchronization
sections.content:
OSPF's flooding algorithm ensures that all routers in an area receive all LSAs and maintain identical databases. When a router originates or receives an LSA, it floods the LSA to all neighbors except the one it was received from, using Link State Update packets sent over adjacencies. Upon receipt, a router checks if the LSA is newer than the copy in its database using the sequence number and age. If newer, it is installed in the database and flooded onward. If older, it is ignored. If a received LSA has the same sequence number as one in the database, the router sends back a Link State Acknowledgment.

The flooding procedure is reliable: routers retransmit LSAs to neighbors until they receive acknowledgments. This ensures that even if a packet is lost, the LSA will eventually be received. The algorithm detects duplicate transmissions and ensures that LSAs are not flooded back out the interface they arrived on, preventing loops and unnecessary traffic.
sections.eli5: When a router learns about a network change, it forwards the news to all its neighbors. Each neighbor checks if the news is new, and if so, forwards it onward. The news keeps spreading until every router has heard it. Routers keep resending the news until their neighbors confirm receipt.

sections.title: Computing Routes from the Database
sections.content:
Once a router has synchronized its link-state database with its neighbors, it calculates its routing table using the SPF algorithm. For routers within a single area, the algorithm builds a shortest-path tree from the current router using the link-state database, calculating the minimum cost path to every destination in the area.

For inter-area routing, area border routers summarize the topology of their attached areas in summary-LSAs. When a router examines these summary-LSAs from area border routers, it learns the cost to inter-area destinations via each border router, allowing it to select the border router with the lowest total cost for each inter-area destination. For AS external routes, the router examines AS-external-LSAs from AS boundary routers and calculates the total cost as the distance to the originating router plus the external metric, choosing the advertising router with the lowest total cost. When multiple equal-cost routes exist, OSPF uses all of them, distributing traffic across equal-cost paths.
sections.eli5: With the complete map in hand, each router calculates the shortest route to every destination by working out all possible paths. When routes to distant areas come from different boundary routers, the router picks the shortest total journey. If two paths cost the same, it uses both.

sections.title: Authentication and Security
sections.content:
All OSPF protocol exchanges are authenticated, ensuring that only trusted routers can participate in the AS routing. OSPF supports three authentication types. Null authentication provides no security; it simply indicates that authentication is not in use. Simple password authentication includes a clear-text password in each OSPF packet; a router accepts a packet only if the password matches. Cryptographic authentication uses an OSPF authentication key to compute a cryptographic checksum of the packet, protecting against spoofing and packet modification.

Authentication can be configured differently for each subnet or area. Additionally, all OSPF LSAs carry a checksum covering the LSA contents, allowing routers to detect corruption of data in the database. External routes can be tagged by the advertising router, enabling the passing of additional information between routers at the boundary of the AS, such as the origin of an external route or a prepended AS path.
sections.eli5: Before accepting a routing message, a router checks that it came from a trusted source using a password or cryptographic signature. This prevents an intruder from injecting false routing information. Each routing message also carries a checksum to catch accidental corruption.

sections.title: Status and Legacy
sections.content:
RFC 2178 documents OSPF version 2 as a standards-track protocol. The differences from the earlier RFC 1583 are backward-compatible; implementations of both versions can interoperate. This RFC added enhancements to authentication, support for the Point-to-MultiPoint interface type, overlapping area ranges, refinements to the flooding algorithm, introduction of the MinLSArrival constant to prevent LSA storms, and several other robustness improvements.

RFC 2178 has been superseded by RFC 2328, which consolidates OSPF version 2 and includes additional clarifications and corrections. Implementations should migrate to RFC 2328 for the most current specification.
sections.eli5: This is version 2 of OSPF, published in 1997. It made OSPF faster and more secure than the earlier version while keeping them compatible. A newer version (RFC 2328) replaced it with further improvements.
